stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the novel shows both parts?
stimulus: The Span at Harlow Ferry, a 1911 novel by Edith Marrow, follows Thomas Reade, an engineer building a steel bridge across a wide and fast river. Marrow presents Reade as a man whose care for his calculations does not slip even when his body is worn out: ______
choices: "He was so weary by nightfall that he fell asleep at the drafting table before his supper came."
"Every rivet on the east pier, he insisted, must be counted, tested, and written in the ledger."
"Though his eyes ached and the lamp burned low, he checked each figure for the load a third time."
"From the site office he watched the river slide past, calm and grey beneath the morning fog."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Reade is careful with his calculations, AND he stays careful while worn out. Choice C shows both. His aching eyes and the low lamp show exhaustion, and checking each figure a third time shows care. This is the core step of every literary-quotation question: split the claim into its parts, then find the one line that shows all of them.

A.why: This line shows that Reade is worn out, which is half the claim. But he falls asleep instead of working, so it shows nothing about his care for his calculations. You probably matched the tired mood and stopped checking.

B.why: This line shows that Reade is careful, which is half the claim. Nothing in it says he is tired. You probably saw the precision and forgot the 'even when worn out' part.

D.why: This line comes from the right setting, the bridge site, but it describes the river. It shows neither Reade's care nor his tiredness. Being in the right scene is not the same as supporting the claim.

stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the book shows both parts?
stimulus: Letters from the Organ Loft (1874) collects the letters of Samuel Penrose, choirmaster of a small country church. Writing about the hymns his parish had sung for generations, Penrose treats them with real admiration, yet he admits they are very hard for his singers to perform: ______
choices: "The old tunes are lovely, I grant you, but no choir of mine can reach their highest notes."
"I have loved these hymns since I first heard them sung as a small boy in the cathedral at Wells."
"Our new soprano struggles with nearly every line the vicar chooses for the Sunday service."
"The organ itself was built in 1790, and it still has to be tuned by hand each spring."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Penrose admires the old hymns, AND he finds them hard for his choir to sing. Choice A shows both. 'Lovely' shows admiration, and 'no choir of mine can reach their highest notes' shows the difficulty. This habit of checking a line against every part of the claim is what literary-quotation questions test.

B.why: This line shows only admiration. It says nothing about the hymns being hard to sing. You probably matched the warm tone and stopped there.

C.why: This line shows a singing difficulty, but it is about one singer and whatever hymns the vicar picks, not the old hymns. It also shows no admiration. You probably matched the word 'struggles' to 'hard to perform.'

D.why: This line is from the right place, the church, but it is about the organ. It shows neither part of the claim. Overlapping with the topic is not support.

stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the novel shows both parts?
stimulus: Clara Haddon's 1896 novel The Ninth Loom follows Nell Ashby, a weaver at a cotton mill in northern England. Haddon portrays Nell as a worker who resents how little the mill pays her but still takes pride in the cloth she produces: ______
choices: "She cared nothing for the mill or its cloth, and lived only for the bell that let her go."
"The pay was a disgrace, she said, yet no cloth in the whole shed was finer than hers."
"Eleven shillings a week, she muttered, would hardly keep a cat in milk and coal."
"The foreman walked the long rows each morning, swinging his ring of iron keys."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Nell resents her low pay, AND she is proud of her work. Choice B shows both. 'The pay was a disgrace' is the resentment, and 'no cloth in the whole shed was finer than hers' is the pride. When you can name both parts before reading the choices, the right line is the only one that shows both.

A.why: This line says Nell cares nothing for the cloth, which is the opposite of the pride the claim describes. You may have read it as general unhappiness with the mill and accepted it.

C.why: This line clearly shows resentment about pay, which is half the claim. It says nothing about pride in her work. Matching only the stronger, more vivid half is the classic trap here.

D.why: This line comes from the right scene, the mill floor, but it describes the foreman, not Nell. It shows neither part of the claim.

stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the novel shows both parts?
stimulus: In The Word-Gatherer, a 1923 novel by Hugh Tallis, a young scholar travels to a remote village to record its dialect. Tallis shows the narrator as eager to collect the villagers' unusual words while also worried that they will feel mocked by his interest: ______
choices: "Each evening I copied out the strange words I had overheard that day in the tavern."
"The village lay at the end of a muddy lane, three long miles from the nearest station."
"I cared little what they thought of me, so long as my notebook filled with new words."
"I longed to write down every odd word they used, yet feared they would think I laughed."
explanation: The claim has two parts: the narrator is eager to collect words, AND he worries the villagers will feel mocked. Choice D shows both. 'Longed to write down every odd word' is the eagerness, and 'feared they would think I laughed' is the worry. The skill here is the same one a full literary-quotation question needs: one line, every part of the claim.

A.why: This line shows the narrator eagerly collecting words, which is half the claim. It shows no worry about the villagers. You probably stopped once the collecting matched.

B.why: This line describes the setting, not the narrator's feelings. It shows neither part of the claim, though it comes from the same story.

C.why: This line shows eagerness to collect words, but 'I cared little what they thought of me' is the opposite of worrying about the villagers' feelings. You may have matched the notebook detail and missed the reversal.

stem: Which line shows BOTH parts of the claim: that Whitcombe feared catching the disease AND that she kept caring for her patients?
stimulus: Clara Whitcombe's memoir *Notes from the Isolation Ward* (1894) recalls her years as a nurse in a hospital for patients with smallpox. This was before most hospital staff had been vaccinated against the disease. In the book, Whitcombe gives a frank account of the long night shifts, the crowded wards and the doctors she worked beside. One historian claims that Whitcombe presents herself as afraid of catching the disease but still unwilling to abandon the people in her care.
choices: "My hands shook whenever I thought of the fever reaching me at last."
"The ward was cold, and the lamps had burned low by midnight."
"Each morning I dreaded the ward, and each morning I walked into it."
"I sat beside the sick through every long hour of the night."
explanation: Cut the claim down to its two parts: (1) she was afraid of catching the disease, AND (2) she kept caring for patients anyway. Then put each line into plain words. Choice C says "I was scared of the ward every day, and I went in every day anyway." "Dreaded" gives you the fear, and "walked into it" gives you the staying. It is the only line that shows both parts. This check underlies every literary-quotation question on the test: before you pick a line, name each part of the claim and confirm the line shows all of them, not just one.

A.why: This is the subtype's main trap. You saw the fear ("my hands shook") and stopped checking. Nothing in the line shows her staying with or caring for anyone, so it gives you only half of the claim.

B.why: This line comes from the right setting, a night on the ward, and that probably made it feel relevant. In plain words, though, it only says the room was cold and dark. It shows neither her fear nor her care for patients, so it supports neither part of the claim.

D.why: This is the same half-claim trap from the other side. Sitting with the sick all night shows she was devoted to them, but nothing here says she was afraid. Without the fear, the line can't show the "afraid but still stayed" claim.
